ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Portland, OR
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Portland, OR for hulls, tanks, vessels, piping and bridge steel. Technicians mobilize. Quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Portland, Oregon
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Portland, Oregon, for ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection on ship hulls and tanks, pressure vessels, process and utility piping, storage tanks and structural steel. Readings are taken to a written procedure, interpreted against the code or the owner's minimum thickness, and reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III before the report is issued. Send us the asset list and access details for a Portland UT quote.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Portland

Portland is a river port, and most of its steel sits near water. The Willamette River carries deep-draft ships to a harbor with terminals for containers, autos, liquid bulks, grain and mineral bulks, and the Swan Island industrial area, about four and a half miles downriver from downtown, holds a large ship repair yard with floating drydocks, wide fabrication bays and heavy cranes. Each of those places generates ultrasonic work. A hull that has been in salt and fresh water for years needs plate thickness mapped before steel is renewed. A fuel or liquid-bulk tank needs its shell and floor plates measured before the owner decides on repair. A crane runway girder, a steel bridge member or a fabricated structural frame needs its welds examined before it is loaded.

Inland from the river, Portland's industrial base also includes metal fabrication, equipment manufacturing, food and beverage processing with steam and ammonia systems, and the semiconductor and electronics plants in the western suburbs, which run stainless process piping and utility systems. Boilers and unfired pressure vessels in all of these plants fall under Oregon's boiler and pressure vessel rules, which makes thickness data a recurring need rather than a one-time survey.

What ultrasonic testing measures, and what it cannot see

A contact ultrasonic probe sends a short sound pulse into the steel and times the echo from the far surface or from a flaw. For thickness testing, that time becomes remaining wall once the instrument is calibrated to the sound velocity of the material. For weld examination, an angled probe sends shear waves through the weld volume so that lack of fusion, cracks, slag and incomplete penetration reflect sound back to the probe. The method sees inside the metal, which is why it is the usual choice when a surface method cannot answer the question.

It has limits that matter on Portland jobs. Sound will not cross an air gap, so a rough, scaled or heavily coated surface has to be prepared or the reading is lost. Pitted wall can return a reading from the shoulder of a pit rather than its bottom, so a thickness gauge reports the thinnest spot under the probe, not the deepest pit nearby. Coarse-grained castings and some stainless welds scatter sound and reduce sensitivity. A planar flaw lying parallel to the sound beam can be missed, which is why weld procedures call for scanning from both sides and at more than one angle where geometry allows.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Portland work

The governing document depends on what the steel is. Pressure equipment built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 uses Appendix 12 for ultrasonic examination of welds, with the technique written to ASME Section V Article 4. Process piping under ASME B31.3 follows paragraph 344.6 for ultrasonic examination, with acceptance in Table 341.3.2. Structural steel in buildings and cranes is examined to AWS D1.1, which has its own ultrasonic acceptance rules for groove welds, and steel highway bridges are covered by AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code that state transportation departments call up. Thickness measurement itself is described in ASME Section V Article 5 and standardized in ASTM E797 for contact pulse-echo gauging. In-service tanks and piping are assessed against API 653 and API 570, where the owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility and Atlantis supplies the thickness and flaw data.

Oregon adds its own layer. The state's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Specialty Code, in its 2024 edition, adopts the 2023 National Board Inspection Code, the 2023 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, and ASME B31.1 and B31.3 piping codes with Oregon amendments. Under the state's inspection rule, power boilers are inspected yearly and unfired vessels subject to internal corrosion are inspected internally and externally every two years, so the readings feed an inspector who works to a fixed calendar. See the Oregon Building Codes Division boiler and pressure vessel page for the current code book.

How the examination is done

For thickness work, the technician first sets up on a step block of the same alloy, covering the thickness range of the job, and checks the instrument at the start and again at the end of the shift. On corroded steel a dual-element probe is the normal choice because its transmit and receive crystals are angled, which handles rough and pitted surfaces better than a single crystal. The technician watches the A-scan trace, not just the number, so a doubled echo on thin wall or a reading that jumps between two values gets noticed. Readings are taken at marked grid points or at the condition monitoring locations the owner already uses, and the same points are used each campaign so trends are meaningful.

For welds, the setup is an angle-beam probe, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees, with a reference level built from side-drilled holes in a block of the same thickness. Scanning covers the full weld and the heat-affected zone from the faces the geometry allows, with the sensitivity raised for scanning and indications evaluated at the reference level. Hot surfaces, for example an operating steam line, need high-temperature probes and couplant and a temperature correction, because sound speed in steel and in the probe wedge changes with heat.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis has no office in Portland. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. They are qualified under the company's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II sets up and calibrates the equipment and performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports. Procedure approval and report review come from our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III certification in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If your own program already has a written practice, the work can be done to your procedure instead, and our Level III consulting can review it before the job starts.

Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Those standards cover the management system, not the personnel qualification, which is handled under the written practice.

What a Portland UT report contains

  • Component identification: equipment number, line number or hull frame, with a sketch or thickness grid showing where each reading was taken.
  • The procedure number and revision, the code or owner specification used, and the acceptance criteria applied.
  • Instrument, probe, wedge, couplant and block identification, with the calibration checks made at the start and end of the work.
  • Technician name and certification level, and the Level III who reviewed the report.
  • Thickness readings against nominal and against the required minimum, with the thinnest reading highlighted rather than buried in a table.
  • For welds, each indication with location along the weld, depth, length and amplitude against the reference level, and an accept or reject call against the named criteria.
  • Limitations: surfaces that could not be scanned, areas with poor coupling, and anything the technique cannot answer.

A reader who works for an owner, a classification surveyor or an Oregon boiler inspector should be able to find the answer on the first page and the evidence behind it on the rest.

Planning a UT job in Portland

Weather drives much of the planning. Portland's wet season runs through the cooler months, and rain on outdoor steel, a wet drydock floor or a damp hull washes away couplant and leaves surfaces that need drying and cleaning before readings are repeatable. Cold mornings slow gel couplant and can chill a probe, so a technician who calibrates in a warm truck and then works on cold plate will see small errors unless the block is brought to the working temperature. Summer is dry and a better window for tank and bridge work outdoors.

Access is the other constraint. Ship repair yards have their own safety orientation and hot-work permits, and work in a tank or hold may need confined-space entry, ventilation and an attendant. Harbor terminals and plants on the river have badging requirements. Bridge members may need lift access or lane closures arranged by the owner. Tell us the access method, the surface condition and any insulation or coating that must be removed in advance, and the crew can bring the right probes, blocks and couplant on the first trip, which keeps travel to a Portland site to a single mobilization where possible.

UT, MT or PT for your Portland job

Choose ultrasonic testing when the question is how thick the wall is, or whether a weld is sound all the way through. Choose magnetic particle testing in Portland when you need surface and near-surface cracks found quickly on carbon or low-alloy steel welds, such as crane runway welds or lifting lugs. Choose liquid penetrant testing in Portland for surface-breaking flaws on stainless steel, aluminum and copper-nickel, where magnetic methods do not work. Many jobs use two: thickness first to decide where to grind, then a surface method to prove a crack is gone. The national page on ultrasonic testing sets out the full service, and the ultrasonic testing guide explains the physics in plain language.

Radiographic testing is a different case. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, but ultrasonic examination can serve as the volumetric method when the code and the owner allow it.

Training your own UT technicians

If you would rather build in-house capability, the UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training pages describe the courses, and our NDT training page for Portland explains how theory, simulator work and the hands-on practical at your own facility fit together under your written practice. The ultrasonic testing simulator lets a trainee practice scanning and interpretation before touching a real weld.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing cost in Portland and how is it scoped?
faq.a: Cost depends on the number of locations, the surface condition, access and how far the crew travels, so each job is quoted from your asset list. Send equipment details, drawings if you have them, and the access method, and we scope the readings.

faq.q: Can you do ultrasonic thickness testing on a ship hull at a Portland shipyard?
faq.a: Yes, technicians can gauge hull plate and tank boundaries in a drydock or alongside. If a classification society will credit the readings to a survey, confirm that society's requirements for the gauging firm before the job, since owner-use readings and class-credited readings are not the same thing.

faq.q: How do you inspect welds with ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: A technician uses an angle-beam probe calibrated on a block with side-drilled holes, scans the full weld and heat-affected zone, and evaluates indications against the reference level and the acceptance criteria of the governing code, such as ASME Section VIII or AWS D1.1.

faq.q: Which code applies to ultrasonic examination of steel bridge welds in Oregon?
faq.a: Highway steel bridges are normally governed by AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, as called up in the owner's contract. The agency's specifications can add requirements, so we work from the contract documents and the owner's procedure.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing find corrosion under insulation or coatings?
faq.a: Thickness can be measured through intact coatings in some cases, but insulation has to be opened at the reading location. Readings taken through coating need a verified technique, so the procedure states whether the coating is removed or measured through.

faq.q: Do you need to take equipment out of service for UT in Portland?
faq.a: Often not for external thickness testing, since readings are taken from the outside of a vessel, pipe or tank shell while it operates, within the temperature limits of the probe. Internal access is only needed for items where the outside cannot be reached.

faq.q: What does Oregon require for pressure vessel inspection?
faq.a: Oregon's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Specialty Code and the state inspection rule set the inspection intervals by equipment type, and the inspector who signs is separate from the NDE technician. Our thickness data supports that inspector's decisions.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or crew in Portland?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Portland. Technicians are mobilized to your site from outside the area for the agreed scope, and travel is planned with you as part of the quote. We reply to enquiries within one business day.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my Portland weld?
faq.a: Sometimes. Some codes allow ultrasonic examination as an alternative for volumetric examination, but the substitution must be agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before the work, and not every weld or code permits it.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection in Portland, OR | MT Testing
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) in Portland, OR on crane steel, hull and bridge welds, lifting gear and fabrications. Technicians travel to site. Quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Portland, Oregon
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends magnetic particle technicians to Portland, Oregon, to examine welds, castings, forgings and in-service steel for surface and near-surface cracks. The work covers crane runways and lifting gear, ship repair welds, steel bridge details, fabricated frames and pressure equipment repairs. Examinations follow a written procedure, indications are marked and recorded, and an ASNT NDT Level III reviews the report. Request a Portland magnetic particle quote with the part list, access and governing code.

Where mag particle testing is used around Portland

Most of Portland's heavy steel is ferromagnetic carbon and low-alloy plate, which is exactly what this method suits. On the Willamette River, the Swan Island repair yard works on large vessels in floating drydocks, and crane rails, bollards, hull weld repairs, rudder and shaft support structures and lifting padeyes all produce magnetic particle work. The harbor's terminals handle containers, autos, liquid bulks, grain and break-bulk cargo, so container cranes, ship-to-shore rails, bulk conveyor frames and rail-served loading structures carry fatigue-sensitive welds that are inspected on a regular schedule.

Fabrication shops across the metro area build structural steel, vessels, trailers, heavy equipment frames and plate assemblies. Those shops use magnetic particle inspection for weld toes, root grind-outs, gouged-and-welded repair areas and lifting attachments before parts ship. Owners of cranes, hoists, forklifts and trucks use it to check for fatigue cracks at pin bores, boom welds and frame joints that visual examination alone can miss.

Rail is part of the picture too. The largest container terminal has an on-dock railyard, and rail-served bulk and auto terminals sit along the same river corridor, so rail-mounted equipment, loading arms and trackside steel add to the list of structures whose welds are examined on a schedule. Owners often combine several of these items into one visit so the technician and yoke are used efficiently.

What the method finds and what it misses

Magnetic particle inspection works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper-nickel and titanium are not magnetic, so those parts need a penetrant examination instead. The technician magnetizes the part so that magnetic flux crosses the expected crack direction. A crack interrupts the field and pulls a small leakage field to the surface, which attracts fine iron particles and shows as a sharp line. The method is fast and sensitive to tight surface-breaking cracks, including fatigue cracks, toe cracks, laps and seams, and to some flaws just below the surface.

The depth of sensitivity falls off quickly, so buried flaws are not reliably found. Orientation matters, because a crack lying parallel to the field produces almost no leakage; the code therefore requires two examinations with the field at roughly right angles. Paint, scale and heavy weld spatter weaken indications and have to be dealt with before examination. Sharp geometry changes, such as thread roots and keyways, can create non-relevant indications that the technician has to tell apart from cracks.

Codes and acceptance criteria for MT in Portland

The technique is written to ASME Section V Article 7, and the acceptance criteria come from the construction code. For pressure vessels, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 sets methods and acceptance. For process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 sets the method and Table 341.3.2 sets what is acceptable. For structural steel, AWS D1.1 covers the examination of welds, and AWS D1.5 applies to steel highway bridges. ASTM E709 is the guide to the method and ASTM E1444 is the practice for magnetic particle testing. For equipment repaired in service, the National Board Inspection Code sets the rules for repairs and alterations, and Oregon has adopted the 2023 edition of that code in its 2024 Boiler and Pressure Vessel Specialty Code, effective October 1, 2024. The Oregon Building Codes Division publishes the current code book. If the repair or inspection is covered by API 653 or API 570, the owner's authorized inspector accepts the work and Atlantis provides the NDE results.

How a magnetic particle examination is carried out

In the field, the most common tool is the electromagnetic yoke. Under ASME Section V Article 7, an alternating-current yoke must show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. The technician checks the lift on a steel test weight, cleans the weld and an adjacent band of base metal, places the yoke across the weld, applies particles, and then repeats with the yoke rotated about ninety degrees. Prods are used where yokes cannot reach and only where the code allows them, since arcing can burn the surface.

Particles come in two forms. Dry powder in a contrasting color is applied by hand bulb for field welds and works well on warm, dry surfaces. Wet particles in a liquid carrier give a stronger indication on fine cracks; fluorescent wet particles are examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, while visible wet particles can be checked in good white light. In shops, a stationary bench with coil and central conductor circular magnetization is used for small parts and forgings. After examination, parts that will go back into service, be welded or sit near sensitive equipment may need demagnetizing, and the technician checks the residual field with a gauss meter.

Personnel, procedures and oversight

Atlantis has no office in Portland. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the scope you agree. They work under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, in which a Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. That Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, whose ASNT NDT Level III qualification covers UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. We can also work to your own written practice and procedure; if you need help drafting one, see our written practice development service. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

Judging indications and what happens after a finding

Every mark that appears is first sorted into relevant or non-relevant. A relevant indication comes from a real discontinuity; a non-relevant one comes from a change in section, a magnetic writing mark or a sharp edge, and the technician proves which it is by cleaning and re-examining, or by changing the magnetizing direction. Relevant indications are then described by shape. Under ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, an indication whose length is more than three times its width is a linear indication, and linear indications in a finished weld are generally unacceptable, while rounded indications are judged against size and spacing limits. The report states the criterion used so the reader can follow the decision.

When a crack is found, the usual next step is to mark its ends, grind it out under an agreed repair procedure, and re-examine the ground area to confirm the crack is gone before any weld repair is made. The repaired weld is then examined again by the same method. Keeping that loop on one visit saves a second mobilization to Portland, so we ask for the repair procedure and the welder's availability in advance when the job is likely to produce findings.

What the MT report shows

  • Part or weld identification, material and surface condition at the time of examination.
  • Procedure number and revision, and the code and acceptance table applied.
  • Equipment: yoke or bench, particle type and lot, carrier, and the checks made on lifting power, particle concentration and lighting.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III reviewer.
  • Each indication with location, orientation and length, a photograph where practical, and the accept or reject decision.
  • Whether the part was demagnetized and the residual field reading.
  • Limits of coverage, such as areas hidden by attachments.

Planning an MT job in Portland

Portland weather affects magnetic particle work in specific ways. Rain and mist on outdoor steel are a problem for dry powder, which clumps on wet surfaces, and wet suspensions can be diluted. Crews bring shelters and drying equipment when they expect damp conditions, or schedule outdoor work for drier months. Cold mornings do not stop the method, but the carrier liquid and the technician's checks need to remain in the range the procedure allows, and very hot or very cold parts are handled with a procedure written for them. For fluorescent work, the area must be dark enough, so work in a bright yard or drydock often needs a tent or a move indoors.

Plant and yard access also shapes the plan. Marine and terminal sites have their own orientation, badging and hot-work permits, and cranes and elevated structures need lifts or scaffolds in place before the technician arrives. Tell us the surface coating, the weld type and thickness, and the preferred time window, and we plan one trip around them. A short call before the visit settles which areas need paint removed, which need scaffolding, and which can be examined as they stand. Sending photographs of the areas to be examined avoids surprises with insulation, fireproofing or tight access.

Choosing between MT, PT and UT in Portland

If the part is carbon or low-alloy steel and the question is cracks at the surface, magnetic particle testing is usually the quickest and most sensitive answer. If the part is stainless steel, aluminum or a copper-nickel alloy, use liquid penetrant testing in Portland. If the question is wall thickness or internal weld quality, use ultrasonic testing in Portland. The national magnetic particle testing page covers the service in general, and the MT versus PT comparison helps when the choice is not clear.

Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States; where volumetric examination is needed, ultrasonic examination may be an option if your code and owner agree.

Training MT technicians in Portland

Teams that inspect their own cranes and fabrications can train technicians through MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training. Our Portland NDT training page explains how the course, the simulator and the hands-on practical fit your written practice. For background on the Article 7 requirements, read the ASME Section V Article 7 explainer.

faq.q: What is magnetic particle inspection and when is it used in Portland?
faq.a: It is a method that finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks in ferromagnetic steel by magnetizing the part and applying fine iron particles. In Portland it is used on crane steel, ship repair welds, fabrications and lifting gear.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be used on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: No, because the method needs the part to be strongly magnetic. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper-nickel are not, so liquid penetrant testing is used instead for surface-breaking flaws on those materials.

faq.q: When would a Portland job use fluorescent wet particles instead of dry powder?
faq.a: Dry powder in a contrasting color suits field welds on warm, dry steel. Wet particles, often fluorescent and viewed under UV-A light in a dark area, give a stronger indication on fine cracks and suit shop work or critical welds.

faq.q: Does Portland rain stop magnetic particle inspection outdoors?
faq.a: Rain affects dry powder and can dilute wet suspensions, so crews use shelters and dry the surface before testing, or schedule work for drier weather. We discuss the weather plan with you when we agree the scope.

faq.q: Why does the procedure require two directions of magnetization?
faq.a: A crack that lies parallel to the magnetic field gives almost no leakage and may not show. Examining twice with the field at roughly right angles lets cracks in any direction produce an indication.

faq.q: Is demagnetizing required after MT?
faq.a: Only when a residual field would interfere with later welding, machining, instruments or service. The technician checks the residual field with a meter and demagnetizes the part if the procedure or the owner requires it.

faq.q: Which codes govern magnetic particle testing of welds in Oregon?
faq.a: The method comes from ASME Section V Article 7, with acceptance taken from the construction code, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1. Oregon adopts the National Board Inspection Code for repairs of pressure equipment.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or technicians stationed in Portland?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Portland. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, with travel planned in the quote. We reply to every enquiry within one business day.

faq.q: Can you examine crane runway welds and lifting lugs?
faq.a: Yes. Crane runways, padeyes, lifting lugs and fatigue-prone details on carbon steel are common magnetic particle work. Send the drawings or photographs and the load rating documents so the examination matches the code or manufacturer requirement.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Portland, OR | PT Testing
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Portland, OR for stainless, aluminum and copper-nickel welds, tanks, piping and castings. Technicians mobilize to site. Quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Portland, Oregon
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to Portland, Oregon, for dye penetrant inspection of welds and parts that magnetic methods cannot handle: stainless steel tanks and piping, aluminum fabrications, copper-nickel seawater systems, nickel alloys, castings and machined components. Each examination follows a written procedure, with the penetrant materials, temperature and acceptance criteria recorded in a report reviewed by an ASNT NDT Level III. Ask for a Portland penetrant testing quote and include the material, surface finish and governing code.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Portland

Portland has a lot of non-magnetic metal. Along the Willamette River, ship repair and marine fabrication involve aluminum structures, stainless fittings and copper-nickel seawater piping, all of which need penetrant examination after weld repair. The city's food, beverage and dairy processors run stainless vessels and sanitary piping, and the semiconductor and electronics plants in the western suburbs use stainless and specialty alloy process systems. The metro area's metal fabricators build stainless tanks, aluminum frames and pressure parts that must be accepted before they leave the shop. Utilities, water treatment plants and hydroelectric facilities on the Columbia and its tributaries have bronze, stainless and alloy components that need periodic surface examination.

Penetrant testing is also the method of choice for crack checks on machined and cast parts. Pump shafts, valve bodies, impellers, forgings and fittings are common work, and so are weld repairs where grinding has removed a defect and the owner wants proof that no surface-breaking flaw remains.

What penetrant testing finds, and what it cannot find

Liquid penetrant testing finds only flaws that are open to the surface. A low-viscosity liquid is applied, allowed to enter any crack, pore or lap by capillary action, and then the excess is removed. A developer draws the trapped liquid back out as a visible mark. Because the method relies on the liquid entering the flaw, it works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not, and it is sensitive to tight cracks that are hard to see by eye.

Anything that blocks the opening defeats it. Smeared metal from grinding or machining, paint, oil, scale, weld spatter and dried cleaner residue can all close a crack mouth, so surface preparation and cleaning decide the result. Porous materials absorb penetrant and give false background. A flaw that is entirely below the surface will not show at all, which is why a weld that needs internal examination is sent for ultrasonic testing instead. The technician also has to tell relevant indications from non-relevant ones, such as a mark at a sharp edge or a scratch.

Codes and acceptance criteria

Technique requirements come from ASME Section V Article 6, and the acceptance criteria come from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 covers penetrant examination of pressure vessel welds. ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 covers process piping, with acceptance in Table 341.3.2. AWS D1.1 and D1.6 apply to structural steel and stainless welds. ASTM E165 is the practice for liquid penetrant testing in general industry, and ASTM E1417 covers the practice for penetrant examination of materials and the performance of the penetrant systems themselves. On stainless steel and nickel alloys, the procedure also limits the halogen and sulfur content of the penetrant materials, because residues can cause corrosion or cracking in service.

In Oregon, repairs to boilers and pressure vessels fall under the state's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Specialty Code, which adopts the 2023 National Board Inspection Code and the 2023 ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code. Where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible under API 510 or API 570, Atlantis reports the examination results and the inspector accepts them. The state's boiler and pressure vessel page lists the current code book.

How the examination is done

The technician starts with the surface. Weld spatter and scale are removed, grinding smear is etched or cleaned away where the procedure requires it, and the part is degreased and dried. Penetrant materials are chosen by the job. Visible dye systems, usually red penetrant with white developer, suit field work in good light. Fluorescent systems are more sensitive, and they are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, so they are used for critical parts and shop work. Penetrant can be water washable, solvent removable or removed after a separate emulsifier step; solvent-removable kits are the field standard because they are portable.

The penetrant is applied by spray, brush or dip and left for the dwell time set in the procedure. Excess is removed carefully, wiping in one direction with lightly dampened cloths, since over-wiping pulls penetrant from shallow flaws. A thin, even coat of developer is applied, and the part is examined after the developing time. The technician records indications with location and size, and photographs them. Afterward the part is cleaned so that residues do not interfere with later welding or service.

Temperature, damp air and other Portland conditions

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the standard temperature range for the part and the penetrant materials at 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside that range, the procedure has to be qualified for the temperature used. Portland's cool, wet months bring cold mornings and damp surfaces. Condensation on a tank wall or hull plate is enough to hold water in a crack and keep penetrant out, so the technician checks the metal temperature with a contact thermometer and dries the surface before starting. Warming the part with a heat source or moving it indoors is often the simplest fix. In summer, shaded surfaces stay in range, but direct sun on dark metal can push it above the limit and make penetrant dry too quickly.

Developer film thickness is also controlled, since a thick coat hides small indications and a thin one gives too little contrast. Aerosol cans and developer should be stored at moderate temperature, and fluorescent work outdoors calls for a tent or dark room. Rain stops the job, because water dilutes the penetrant and ruins the developer film.

Cleaning chemistry deserves a word. Solvent cleaners and removers must be compatible with the base metal and with any product the equipment will later contain, and they must evaporate completely before penetrant is applied, because a wet surface blocks entry. Portland's humid cool-season air slows evaporation, so the technician allows extra drying time and checks the surface rather than assuming it is ready. Cleaning cloths are replaced often, since a dirty cloth redeposits oil on the weld.

Who does the work

Atlantis has no office in Portland. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, working under the company's written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT NDT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Procedure approval and report review rest with Anoop Rayavarapu, who is qualified as an ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If your plant already has a penetrant procedure, we can work to it, and our Level III consulting can review or update it. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

Materials common in Portland and how they change the procedure

Stainless steel in food and beverage plants is often welded as sanitary tube, where the inside of a joint is not reachable and the outside is polished. Penetrant on a polished weld is easy to read, but the technician must remove every trace of it afterward because residues in a product line are not acceptable. Aluminum used in marine and fabricated structures smears easily under a grinder or wire brush, and a smeared surface can hide a crack completely, so the procedure often requires light etching or careful mechanical cleaning before penetrant goes on. Copper-nickel seawater piping and bronze valves clean up well, but oily deposits from the water side must be degreased first.

Where the work is inside a tank, a hold or a vessel, the solvent cleaner and penetrant sprays are flammable and give off vapors, so the plan includes ventilation, an attendant and ignition-source control, arranged with the owner before entry. Spray kits generate waste cloths and cans, and the owner's disposal rules apply on site.

Reading indications and re-examination

Penetrant indications grow as the penetrant bleeds out of the flaw into the developer, so the technician watches the surface during the developing time and again at the end. A crack tends to appear as a sharp line, porosity as small round dots, and a lap as a short curved mark. Broad, fuzzy staining usually means poor cleaning, not a flaw. If an indication is doubtful, the area is cleaned and the whole process repeated. After a repair, the ground area is re-examined by penetrant before any weld metal is added, and then the finished repair is examined again against the acceptance table in the construction code.

What the PT report contains

  • Identification of the weld, part or area examined, with a sketch where useful.
  • Material, surface condition and surface temperature at the time of examination.
  • Procedure number and revision, penetrant, remover and developer brand and batch, and the process type used.
  • Dwell time and developing time, and the lighting conditions.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III reviewer.
  • Each indication with position and size, and the accept or reject decision against the named criteria.
  • Any areas that could not be examined, and post-cleaning done.

Choosing between PT, MT and UT in Portland

Choose penetrant testing for any non-porous material where the concern is surface cracks, particularly stainless steel, aluminum and copper-nickel, or when geometry makes magnetizing awkward. For carbon steel where speed is important, magnetic particle inspection in Portland is faster. For thickness and internal weld quality, use ultrasonic inspection in Portland. The national penetrant testing page describes the service as a whole, and ASME Section V Article 6 explained goes into the technique rules.

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, so where you need a volumetric check on a weld, ultrasonic testing is the alternative if the code and owner permit it.

Training penetrant technicians in Portland

Companies that want their own penetrant capability can train through PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and practice on the penetrant testing simulator before working on production parts. The Portland NDT training page explains the course, simulator and employer practical.

faq.q: What is dye penetrant inspection used for in Portland?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks, laps and porosity on non-porous materials. In Portland that means stainless tanks and piping, aluminum structures, copper-nickel seawater systems, castings, and weld repairs where grinding has removed a defect.

faq.q: Can liquid penetrant testing find flaws below the surface?
faq.a: No. The penetrant has to enter the flaw from the surface, so internal flaws are not detected. For internal weld quality, ultrasonic testing is the usual method when the code allows it.

faq.q: What temperature range does penetrant testing allow?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and penetrant materials. Outside it, the procedure must be qualified for that temperature, which matters in Portland's cold, damp months.

faq.q: Does damp weather affect penetrant testing in Portland?
faq.a: Yes. Water or condensation in a crack stops penetrant from entering, so surfaces must be dry, and rain halts the work outdoors. Crews warm and dry the part, use shelters, or move the examination indoors.

faq.q: Why does surface preparation matter so much?
faq.a: Grinding smear, paint, oil, scale and spatter can close the mouth of a crack, so penetrant cannot enter. Cleaning, and where required etching, is therefore part of the procedure, not an optional extra.

faq.q: Is visible or fluorescent penetrant better?
faq.a: Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and is viewed under UV-A light in a dark area, so it suits critical parts and shop work. Visible dye is practical in the field in good light, and the procedure sets which system applies.

faq.q: Why are halogens and sulfur limited on stainless steel and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Residues of those elements in penetrant materials can promote corrosion or cracking in service on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys. Procedures call for low-halogen, low-sulfur materials and thorough post-cleaning on those alloys.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Portland?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Portland. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, with travel planned in the quote, and we reply to enquiries within one business day.

faq.q: Can you examine aluminum welds with penetrant?
faq.a: Yes. Aluminum is not magnetic, so penetrant is the standard surface method for it. The procedure, the material compatibility and the acceptance criteria are set from the construction code or the owner's specification.

rt.description: Searching for radiographic testing in Portland, OR? Atlantis does not perform RT in the US. See UT as an alternative and Level III radiograph review.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Portland, Oregon: What Atlantis Does and Does Not Do
rt.html:
If you searched for radiographic testing in Portland, Oregon, here is the direct answer: Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography uses sealed gamma sources or X-ray equipment, and in the United States it is a licensed activity, regulated by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission under 10 CFR Part 34 or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State. Oregon is an Agreement State with its own radiation control program. That licence is not something Atlantis holds for work here, so we do not shoot, expose or offer radiography in Portland, and we will not pretend otherwise.

What we can do is help you reach the same answer by other routes. The options below keep your weld acceptance, procedure and records on a sound footing while a licensed radiography contractor, chosen by you, handles any exposures that are truly required.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative

For many welds on pressure piping, vessels and structural steel, ultrasonic examination can replace radiography as the volumetric method. Several codes recognize it. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 each allow ultrasonic examination of production welds under stated provisions, and AWS D1.1 separately sets acceptance criteria for ultrasonic examination of groove welds. ASME Section VIII Division 1 allows ultrasonic examination to stand in for radiography only under specific conditions set out in the Code. Ultrasonic testing also finds planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks, which radiography can miss when the flaw is not aligned with the beam.

The key point is that the substitution is never a technician's call. It has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job begins, and it has to be written into the procedure. Our ultrasonic testing service in Portland covers weld examination with angle-beam probes and thickness surveys. For Portland shipyard, tank and bridge steel, UT is often the most practical route in places where clearing an exposure area would stop other trades.

Level III radiograph review and procedure support

A Level III review of radiographic work needs no radiation licence, because it uses images and documents, not a source. The reviewer would be Anoop Rayavarapu, an ASNT NDT Level III with qualifications in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Review of radiographs, in film or digital image form, can be arranged against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. That includes a second read on disputed or borderline indications, a check of the technique sheet, image quality indicators, density and sensitivity records, and a review of the radiography contractor's procedure and written practice before work starts. The aim is to give the owner an independent opinion on whether the images support the acceptance decision.

This service sits within our Level III consulting. It is useful when a Portland fabricator and an owner disagree about a weld, when a project is inheriting records from a previous contractor, or when a quality manager wants a second opinion before releasing a pressure vessel or a piping package.

Radiographic testing training

If you want your own people to understand radiography, the theory side is available. Our radiographic testing Level 2 course covers principles, techniques, image interpretation and code acceptance, taught as theory under SNT-TC-1A. Radiation safety training and licensing remain a separate matter with the regulator and the licensed employer, and the course does not replace them. For Portland teams, the NDT training page for Portland explains how the course, simulator work and the employer's practical fit together.

Other methods Atlantis performs in Portland

For surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, see magnetic particle inspection in Portland. For stainless steel, aluminum and copper-nickel, see penetrant testing in Portland. Technicians are mobilized to your site, since Atlantis has no office in Portland. Tell us about your weld and code and we will say honestly whether UT or a Level III review can serve you.

faq.q: Is radiography available from Atlantis in Portland, Oregon?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is a licensed activity under NRC rules or the rules of an Agreement State, and Atlantis does not offer it here.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my weld?
faq.a: Sometimes, if the construction code allows it and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree before the work. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 have ultrasonic provisions, while Section VIII allows it only under specific conditions.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs taken by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes, an ASNT NDT Level III can review film or digital images and technique records against ASME Section V Article 2 and your code. This is a document review and needs no radiation licence.

faq.q: Do you recommend a radiography contractor in Portland?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. If your scope truly needs exposures, choose a licensed provider under your own procurement and send us the procedure for an independent review if you wish.

faq.q: Is RT training available even though you do not perform RT?
faq.a: Yes. The radiographic testing Level 2 course is a theory course covering principles, image interpretation and what the codes accept. Radiation safety licensing is separate, and the employer remains responsible for certification under its own written practice.
